questions.question: Why is being square part of the usual definition of an inverse matrix here?
options: Rectangular matrices cannot be multiplied by any matrix, in all instances without exception.
Both products $A^{-1}A$ and $AA^{-1}$ must match identity matrices on the appropriate space.
Square matrices always have an inverse.
Only square matrices can have any entries.

options: Every square matrix is invertible regardless of determinant.

questions.question: Is $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ invertible?
options: No, because it has nonzero off-diagonal entries.
Yes, because every $2\times2$ matrix is invertible.

questions.question: How many inverses can an invertible matrix have?

questions.question: How does invertibility connect to solving $Ax=b$?
options: If $A$ is invertible, every $b$ gives no solution.
If $A$ is invertible, $b$ must be zero.
If $A$ is invertible, the solution is forced to be $x=A^{-1}b$.
